passages: Malaria facts & statistics 2025
Malaria continues to disproportionately affect women and children living in poverty, which in turn fuels existing inequities.

In 2024, available malaria funding of US$ 3.9 billion fell far short of the Global Technical Strategy (GTS) target of US$ 9.3 billion by 2025. [MMV echoes the call for stronger investments in innovation and health systems](https://www.mmv.org/newsroom/news-resources-search/who-launches-2025-world-malaria-report-pressure-drug-resistance).
Below are some highlights from the 2025 report.
Malaria remains a serious global health challenge, particularly in the hard-hit African Region.
* An estimated 282 million new malaria cases in 80 endemic countries worldwide in 2024, up from 273 million in 2023.
* Three countries – Ethiopia, Madagascar and Yemen – accounted for 58% of the estimated case increase from 2023 to 2024.
* Ten countries account for 66% of all malaria cases worldwide: Nigeria, DRC, Uganda, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Angola, Tanzania, Cote d’Ivoire, Mali and Burkina Faso.
* Total malaria deaths increased, with 610,000 malaria deaths in 2024 vs. 598,000 deaths reported in 2023.
* The WHO Africa Region accounts for 94% of cases and 95% of deaths globally.
* Three countries – Nigeria (31.9%), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11.7%) and Niger (6.1%) – accounted for half of all deaths in the region.
* In Africa, 75% of malaria deaths were in children under 5 years old.
* Elimination is now within reach in three countries in the Greater Mekong subregion (GMS): Cambodia, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic and Vietnam.
![World Malaria report 2025](/sites/default/files/styles/landscape_16_9_xsmall/public/content/image/casesdeath%20averted.png.jpeg?itok=xYBZf9Qt)
Malaria responses worldwide are preventing illness and saving lives:
* Globally, an estimated 2.3 billion malaria cases and 14 million malaria deaths have been averted since 2000.

* [**Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC)**](https://www.mmv.org/our-work/access-medicines/seasonal-malaria-chemoprevention)continues to scale up, reaching an average of 55 million children in 2025 at high risk of severe malaria in 19 countries.
* **Perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC)** was implemented in at least 8 countries with nearly 1 million children aged under 24 months receiving their first dose of PMC in 2024.
* **Two vaccines are being rolled out**, with a total of 24 countries having introduced them by October 2025 through routine childhood immunization care.

* **Insecticide-treated net (ITN)** use remains generally unchanged, with almost half (47%) of those at risk of malaria sleeping under them. However, significant progress has been made to distribute nets that are more effective at combatting insecticide resistance.
* **Intermittent Preventive Treatment in pregnancy (IPTp)** was stable in 2024 (45% vs. 43% in 2023), which still falls short of the global target of 80%.
### Newstory: See how MMV has been improving equitable access in 2024](https://www.mmv.org/newsroom/news-resources-search/who-launches-its-2024-world-malaria-report-calling-reinvigorated)
## Downloads
Case management for children under the age of 5 has improved, with increased diagnosis and use of [ACTs](https://www.mmv.org/malaria/symptoms-and-treatments/about-artemisinin-and-ACTs).

ACTs are the most effective and widely recommended treatment for uncomplicated malaria – especially for infections caused by *Plasmodium falciparum*, the parasite responsible for most malaria deaths in Africa.

In 2025, MMV and Novartis announced that [Coartem Baby became the first malaria medicine to be authorized for young infants](https://www.mmv.org/newsroom/news-resources-search/coartemr-baby-launches-ghana).
![54 million children received SMC in 2024 (partial data)](/sites/default/files/styles/landscape_16_9_xsmall/public/content/image/SMC_54million.png.jpeg?itok=47dXtQoA)
An average 54 million children received SMC across 19 countries in 2024 (partial data).
### Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC)
* SMC, an MMV-supported intervention, reached on average 56 million children in 19 African countries in 2025.
* Nigeria, which carries the highest malaria burden of any country, accounted for over half of the children who received SMC.
* The number of children receiving a fifth cycle of SMC is gradually increasing.
In 2025, 45% of eligible pregnant women and girls in 34 countries received at least three doses of preventive medicine, which is still below the global target of 80% coverage.

Together with accelerating IPTp uptake, MMV’s [Malaria in Mothers and Babies (MiMBa) initiative](https://www.mmv.org/our-work/malaria-mothers-and-babies-mimba) continues to spearhead equitable access to antimalarials for pregnant women and adolescent girls, who are among the highest at risk of severe illness and death from malaria.

A key priority is to use pregnancy registries and expand clinical research ([project SAFIRE)](https://safire-consortium.org/) to generate safety and dosing evidence for the use of existing antimalarials amongst pregnant women in their first trimester.
Read more about [antimalarials for pregnant women](/node/12231).
![Swipha, African manufacturing](/sites/default/files/styles/landscape_16_9_xsmall/public/content/image/MMV22161.jpg.jpeg?itok=7GKVvLaT)
### Quality-assured African manufacturing

MMV has worked with pharmaceutical manufacturers in Kenya and Nigeria to support them in achieving quality assurance from WHO for the preventive medicines used for SMC and IPTp, which helps ensure medicines are manufactured where they are needed most.

In 2024, Swiss Pharma Nigeria Limited (Swipha), with support from MMV and Unitaid, became the [first Nigerian manufacturer of WHO-prequalified sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine](https://www.mmv.org/newsroom/news-resources-search/first-nigerian-manufacturer-obtains-who-prequalification-key-malaria), used for preventing malaria in children and pregnant women. [Read more about African antimalarial manufacturing](/node/14860).

The burden of malaria, and the challenges to addressing it, are most acute in Africa, where 11 countries bear about two thirds of the world’s malaria burden.
Together, these countries are part of a targeted initiative – “high burden to high impact (HBHI)” – aimed at accelerating progress against the disease.
Between 2017 and 2023, mortality rates in these countries fell by 13%.
Since 2015, nine countries have been certified as malaria free by the World Health Organization (WHO), including five over the past 2 years: Azerbaijan, Belize, Cabo Verde, Egypt and Tajikistan.
Together, they demonstrate that, with sustained commitment and investment, malaria elimination is attainable in all countries.
vii Technological advances hold the promise of further gains.
Malaria remains a formidable challenge.

By working together, tailoring interventions to local settings, harnessing innovation and maintaining a relentless focus, we can regain momentum and move towards our shared vision of a malaria free future.

The pivotal meeting brought together more than 400 stakeholders, including ministers of health and senior representatives from malaria endemic countries in Africa, global health leaders, scientists, civil society and other partners.

At the end of the meeting and in the weeks that followed, ministers of health from the 11 high burden to high impact (HBHI) African countries (Burkina Faso, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ghana, Mali, Mozambique, the Niger, Nigeria, the Sudan, Uganda and the United Republic of Tanzania) signed the Yaoundé Declaration, pledging their “unwavering commitment” to the principle that “no one should die from malaria given the tools and systems available”.
“In signing the Yaoundé Declaration, the Honourable Ministers have helped lay a foundation that will ensure a brighter future for children across Africa.

# World Malaria Report 2024: Accelerating progress and preserving the gains of the fight against malaria
Posted on December 11, 2024
###### By Charles Guissou
Co-Principal Investigator, Institut de Recherche en Sciences de la Santé
Target Malaria Burkina Faso
Today the World Health Organization published its [annual World Malaria Report](https://www.who.int/teams/global-malaria-programme/reports/world-malaria-report-2024).
Since 2000, malaria control efforts have helped avert 2.2 billion cases and 12.7 million deaths worldwide.
In 2023 alone, more than 177 million cases and 1 million deaths were averted globally.
Most cases (80%) and deaths (94%) averted were in the WHO African Region.
Many countries with a low burden of malaria continue to move steadily towards the goal of elimination.
In 2023, more than half (47) of the 83 malaria-endemic countries worldwide reported less than 10 000 cases of the disease.
The African Region continues to bear the heaviest burden of malaria, accounting for an estimated 94% of global cases and 95% of malaria-related deaths in 2023.
Just over half of these deaths occurred in four countries: Nigeria (30.9%), Democratic Republic of the Congo (11.3%), Niger (5.9%) and United Republic of Tanzania (4.3%).
In 2023, there were an estimated 263 million new malaria cases in 83 countries worldwide, up from 252 million in 2022 and 226 million in 2015.
Out of the estimated 263 million malaria cases, an estimated 12,573,000 were in Uganda, 8,139,000 in Burkina Faso and 6,552,000 in Ghana.
Despite some gains in Africa’s malaria response, progress must be accelerated.

Approximately two thirds of global malaria cases and deaths are concentrated in 11 African countries: [Burkina Faso](https://targetmalaria.org/?page_id=12367), Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, [Ghana](https://targetmalaria.org/about-us/where-we-operate/ghana/), Mali, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Sudan, United Republic of Tanzania and [Uganda](https://targetmalaria.org/about-us/where-we-operate/uganda/).

There are many threats to progress made against malaria such as funding gaps, poverty, climate change, humanitarian emergencies such as conflicts, and lack of access to essential services such as treatment and preventative methods. [Mosquito resistance](https://targetmalaria.org/virtual-press-room/press-releases/new-mathematical-modelling-study-demonstrates-gene-drives-could-boost-malaria-control-when-added-to-intervention-packages-including-new-bed-nets-and-vaccines/) to insecticide-treated nets and treatments and the spread of *Anopheles stephensi* among others also raise a concern to stall the progress already made.
Although the challenges are increasing, we have a lot of positive progress as well, such as the WHO-recommended malaria vaccine which 17 countries have introduced through childhood immunization.
Between 2019 and 2023, approximately 2 million children in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi received a malaria vaccine, with many more to follow.
This scale-up of malaria vaccines in Africa is expected to save tens of thousands of young lives every year.

However, the [highest impact will be achieved](https://targetmalaria.org/virtual-press-room/press-releases/new-mathematical-modelling-study-demonstrates-gene-drives-could-boost-malaria-control-when-added-to-intervention-packages-including-new-bed-nets-and-vaccines/) when the vaccines are introduced alongside a mix of other malaria interventions that are tailored to the local context, such as new generation bed nets, drugs and the use of genetic technologies.
At Target Malaria, we are developing gene drive mosquitoes as a future potential vector control tool.
We are adapting a natural genetic mechanism called “gene drive”, to bias the rate of inheritance in order to spread a genetic modification in malaria mosquitoes to make them sterile.

Used jointly with other malaria control tools, gene drive mosquitoes hold the promise of being a self-sustaining and cost-effective method to reduce the population of malaria mosquitoes in the future.
You can read more [information about our work here](https://targetmalaria.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/BrochureA5_Mar2024_En_Digital.pdf).
Although the findings from this year’s report lay bare the heavy burden of malaria in Africa, they also paint a hopeful picture around the opportunities to accelerate progress.
With the right investment, research and development, community engagement and political will, it is possible to reverse the trends and accelerate progress towards malaria elimination.
Now is the time to act.
Read the [key findings from last year’s World Malaria Report report here](https://targetmalaria.org/latest/news/world-malaria-report-2023-key-findings-from-the-report/).

# World malaria report 2025
## Antimalarial drug resistance challenging progress
Each year, WHO’s *World malaria report* provides a comprehensive and up-to-date assessment of trends in malaria control and elimination across the globe.

The 2024 edition reviews investments in malaria programmes and research and assesses progress across all major intervention areas – prevention, diagnosis, treatment, elimination and surveillance – in 80 malaria-endemic countries.
This year’s report spotlights the growing threat of antimalarial drug resistance.

Partial resistance to artemisinin derivatives – the backbone of malaria treatments after failures of chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine​ – has now been confirmed or suspected in at least 8 countries in Africa, and there are potential signs of declining efficacy of some of the drugs that are combined with artemisinin.
![World malaria report 2025](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/ef1842eb-e9f1-4d6e-a083-ccd5a2b54e12/content)
### World malaria report 2025
## Global malaria toll could deepen

Since 2000, 2.3 billion malaria cases and 14 million deaths have been averted worldwide – including 1 million lives saved in 2024 alone – and there has been continued movement towards global elimination goals, with 47 countries and one territory now officially certified as malaria-free by WHO.
Despite these gains, however, malaria remains a serious global health challenge, with an estimated 282 million cases and 610 000 deaths in 2024 – roughly 9 million more cases than the previous year.
The WHO African Region continues to bear the greatest burden, with 11 countries accounting for about two thirds of global cases and deaths.
Progress in reducing the malaria mortality rate nevertheless remains far off track.
New tools saved a million lives from malaria last year but progress under threat as drug resistance rises

invalid_quotes.text: Approximately two thirds of global malaria cases and deaths are concentrated in 11 African countries: Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ghana, Mali, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Sudan, United Republic of Tanzania and Uganda.

reason: Multiple WHO and partner documents state that eleven African countries together account for roughly two‑thirds of worldwide malaria cases (and deaths) in the 2024 period, which satisfies the claim that they accounted for most estimated cases worldwide.
